claims.text: A low-oxygen mixture of refractory-metal powders and Group IV hydride precursors can be prepared by mechanical alloying or blending.
Maintaining pressure below 10^-6 Pa throughout hydride decomposition and extrusion will suppress oxygen uptake.
Heating faster than 50 °C/min to 800–900 °C will decompose the hydrides before significant oxygen diffusion occurs.
Immediate extrusion at 1100–1200 °C permits consolidation without cracking.
TiH2 and ZrH2 thermally decompose and release hydrogen gas.
Hydrogen released during hydride decomposition creates a transient reducing atmosphere in the powder bed.
A short residence time at the decomposition temperature prevents oxygen diffusion from residual impurities or crucible walls.
Released hydrogen scavenges trace oxygen by forming volatile H2O that is removed by the vacuum system.
Oxygen introduced during processing can produce TiO precipitates in a Ti-containing Nb-Mo-Ta-W-based refractory HEA.
Suppressing oxygen uptake prevents precipitation of an alpha-HCP phase in Group-IV-containing refractory HEAs.
Alpha-HCP and TiO phases cause embrittlement and raise the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
The proposed thermal cycle will retain a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The process can alternatively produce a controlled BCC matrix with ordered strengthening precipitates.
Avoiding oxygen-induced phases enhances high-temperature strength by preserving dislocation mobility.
The proposed process will produce material exceeding 99% of theoretical density.
The proposed hydride-based extrusion process will avoid catastrophic cracking.
The consolidated product will contain no detectable alpha-HCP or oxide precipitates.
The resulting Group-IV-containing alloy will have a yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
The hydride-extruded alloy will have better room-temperature ductility than arc-melted counterparts because oxygen-induced embrittlement is absent.
Powder processing of HfNbTaTiZr can cause cracking during swaging, while SPS of mechanically alloyed powder can produce a fully dense but brittle specimen.
